Then McAtee pounces on a bouncing ball in front of Anderson, and is tripped by his former team-mate.

Great work again form James McAtee, carrying the ball down the right touchline and winning a throw-in off Anderson. Gvardiol clears Munoz’s launched delivery. Reaching half-time with a clean sheet will be Glasner’s objective from here.

Haaland with his first shot of the game, but it was an ambitious attempt on the volley, running away from goal to latch on to Guehi’s chipped pass over the top. The striker hit the target, but not enough power to trouble Sels.

Enzo Fernandez has just missed City’s best chance of the game, header over the bar from around six yards. Marc Guehi with the right-footed, inswinging delivery. As things stand, Manchester United are in the relegation zone.

Forest crunch into another tackle in midfield, and Delap wins a free-kick. They have been fantastic to a man so far.

Now Forest have a corner after a teasing Munoz cross. The home team are rampant. Their underlying numbers suggested they were performing like a team closer to the top of the league and they have looked just that so far. From the corner, a snap shot by Murillo is straight at Donnarumma.

James McAtee fires over the bar from the edge of the area when completely unmarked! City all over the place at the moment, Forest are setting traps and they are walking straight into them.

His first goal at the City Ground in a Forest, and what a finish it is.

City made a mess of a loose ball in midfield with Anderson and Ndiaye going all “after you Claude”, and Delap was straight at the heart of their defence again.

You would not know he has been struggling in front of goal, because Delap shifted the ball out of his feet a drilled a powerful shot beyond Donnarumma high into the net.

It can be revealed that Forest’s record signing was on the 55-man list for Thomas Tuchel’s latest England squad, but did not make the cut.

Chants of “you’re going down with United” and “you’re going down with the Derby’ from the Forest fans.

Good defending from Williams up against Ndiaye but Doku helps City keep the squeeze on.

Things break down with a careless Cherki pass in the middle of the pitch, and Forest break down their right through Delap and Munoz.

Forest come into this evening’s game in 19th, but they are just a point behind Crystal Palace and Manchester United, while victory would also take them above Coventry City and up to 16th.

Forest’s results at the City Ground have to improve quickly or this team will be in serious trouble.

Oliver Glasner has played down the significance of his warning to Nottingham Forest’s squad after their defeat at Brentford has had the desired impact.

The Austrian said last weekend there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

Speaking this week, he said: “I didn’t attack anyone directly. We share that we want to be successful and win games. It was not a problem.

“It was much louder outside than I felt it was inside. This is just how I see a relationship has to be. Let’s talk about things if we don’t like things.

“If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

The City manager added: “It is quite easy with him because he recognises any mistake immediately. I’ve spoken to him about it, but I didn’t feel the need to be so deep with him because he already knows and recognises that he has made some mistakes.”

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca said: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

“We know exactly what we are doing well and what we need to improve. It is just a matter of time.”

Elsewhere this afternoon, Martin Odegaard has broken the deadlock at the Emirates to give Arsenal a 1-0 lead over Hull City.

Victory would take Mikel Arteta’s side six points clear of City at the top of the table before this evening’s contest at the City Ground.

Glasner has made two changes to his Forest team following defeat at Brentford last weekend, with Yates and Munoz replacing Ndoye and Aina.

Is this the day the xG gods reward Nottingham Forest? Oliver Glasner’s team sit 19th having won one game all season, but there is no doubt that their performances have been significantly better than results and they might need their luck to turn against Man City team full of firepower.

Despite all of the positive indicators in Forest’s underlying data, Glasner caused some alarm with his comments after last weekend’s defeat at Brentford.

The Austrian said: “We have to accept it’s not good enough. If we lose four of the last five games, it’s not good enough. And that’s why for me, it’s now time that we change things, that I change things, and that’s what I will do.

“I feel now maybe I made too many compromises in some stuff, and it’s always compromises. It’s a clear way. I will tell [the players] what we want to do, what we have to do, and if the players buy in, I think we can have a turnaround, and if not, the sixth manager [since the start of last season] will come in.”

Dangerous words perhaps when you work for Evangelos Marinakis, but John Percy reported this week that Glasner was backed by his players in a squad meeting.

City are smarting from back-to-back defeats by Aston Villa and Brighton, but they created more than enough in both games to claim some sort of result. Nevertheless, there is a persistent sense that their defensive unit remains too marshmellow-like over the course of 38 games, and Forest have the counter-attacking threat to test them.

Glasner has happy memories of playing City, beating them in the 2025 FA Cup final with Crystal Palace, but his Forest reign is in urgent need of a signature victory and performance.

#1023. Mauricio Pochettino denies claims he is 'TOO NICE' to manage Man United - after Jamie Redknapp accused him of going soft with bracelets, high-fives, and a fancy haircut

Published: 12:00 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 13:58 EST, 27 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino has hit back at Jamie Redknapp over his suggestion that Manchester United’s new head coach has become too ‘nice’.

Redknapp made the claim on The Overlap podcast earlier this week, saying of the former Tottenham and Chelsea boss: ‘I've got a little bit of a bee in my bonnet about Pochettino. When I saw Pochettino at Southampton and I saw him at Tottenham, he looked to me like he had that Argentinian dog in him. I look at him now and he's high-fiving everyone, he's got the bracelets on, he's got the barnet. I think he's gone too nice, I do.’

Pochettino appears to have taken issue with Redknapp’s comments because he refuted them unprompted at his press conference on Friday ahead of his first home game against Brentford at Old Trafford this weekend.

‘Sometimes we are confusing two words that maybe have a similar meaning,’ said Pochettino. ‘Nice and good. I am not nice. I am not nice. We have to be good, that is a different thing. I am not nice. I am trying to be good.

‘Be careful because we know when we need to push, when we need to be strong, and when we need to build something to improve the atmosphere and relationship and everything. These two things are different.’

Pochettino has endured an eventful start to life at United, losing his first game 4-0 at Liverpool last weekend after Leny Yoro was shown an early red card – which was later overturned – and then drawing 2-2 with Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League in midweek when United conceded two penalties, had two goals disallowed and saw Youri Tielemans harshly sent off.

Mauricio Pochettino has denied Jamie Redknapp's claim that he is 'too nice' these days

An emotional-looking Redknapp said the Manchester United manager had changed with high-fives, bracelets, and a barnet haircut

‘We need to accept that,’ added Pochettino. ‘What we are going to do? Start to cry? No, be strong, believe, keep going.

‘With this type of situation you can always think, “oh, always things happen against us”, but it's not true. That is not true. These type of things happen. There was a big mistake from the referee against Liverpool, but some things happen. It's happened now with us, it can happen in the future, it happened in the past. The mistake on Wednesday was the same.

‘I need to shut my mouth and say nothing and start from now. When I accepted the invitation to come to Manchester United and start to work in this circumstance, shut my mouth and work 12 hours every day; try to recover the feelings, the emotions, and build our mentality again and really believe in what we are going to do.’

Pochettino accepts it will take time to get the best out of players who have struggled for form and confidence this season as United have slipped into the relegation zone.

‘I think it's easy for us that we arrive one week ago,’ he said. ‘It's easy to arrive here with full energy and being positive and try to build that belief that we need, no?

‘But, of course, for the players it's so tough because we cannot make all that noise go away that is around this football club. But it's not only in this football club, it's in every single club that is not performing well or getting the result that maybe everyone expects. That is it's so tough for the player.

‘What we need to understand is the players need to play. They are going to play tomorrow, and the next one, and the next one, and the next one. The man-management is important, individually and collectively. We need to recover our confidence, our trust and our belief.

‘And, of course, to implement our method little by little. It's not to implement everything. Be careful. What we don't want is to add more pressure. The players are under pressure, we are under pressure, the organisation is under pressure, the fans are under pressure.

‘Everyone is under pressure, but we need to understand that the players need to perform and feel the trust of the people in charge.’

#1020. London’s people-first approach to smart-city development

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Benjamin Plackett is a science journalist based in London.

A virtual-reality model of London’s main financial district, the City of London, has mapped the size and location of every building.Credit: Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images

London has risen to fourth place in the IMD Smart City Index 2026, up from sixth place in 2025 and eighth place in 2024. The index — which is published by IMD, an independent Swiss business institute — draws mostly on residents’ perceptions of infrastructure and technology, not a tally of sensors. That focus on perspective is important, says Trevor Dorling, managing director of DG Cities, a private urban-innovation consultancy spun out of the Royal Borough of Greenwich local authority, which works to make better use of data and introduce new technologies in the southeast London borough.

“We increasingly describe our work as ‘city innovation’ rather than ‘smart cities’, because in many people’s minds ‘smart’ is associated with gadgets and gizmos,” says Dorling. “The aim is to use technology to create better places for people. It shouldn’t be the technologists who define what ‘better’ is, but the communities that live there.”

There is plenty of evidence that London has the resources and knowledge to apply research solutions in such a people-centred way. In the 2026 Nature Index Science Cities table, London is ranked 21st overall, but it jumps to 5th place for health-sciences output, for instance.

The Smart Mobility Living Lab, created by a consortium of public and private organizations, including DG Cities, spans 24 kilometres of roads in Greenwich and the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in Stratford, and is one example of London’s efforts to create societal impact with its innovation.

The area has more than 1,000 different road features, from speed bumps and pedestrian crossings to one-way systems and bridges, that allow companies to test new vehicles and services in busy, real-world complexity. “The driving force for this was the rapid development of self-driving technologies and exploring the opportunities this presented for safety and accessibility, as well as the challenges,” says Dorling.

Trials to test self-driving shuttle buses and delivery vans have put the technology in public view, with residents invited to ride in the test vehicles, an openness that Dorling says has helped overcome scepticism and brought local authorities into the development process at an early stage.

London’s digital-twin projects are similarly pragmatic. The local authority in Harrow (northwest London) uses high-resolution drone imagery to inspect and measure roofs and buildings remotely and to build interactive maps of parks. The council used this approach in April 2026 to make a 3D model of Headstone Manor and Museum — a restored medieval complex and local-history museum — saving £12,000 (US$16,260) by avoiding a conventional roof survey with scaffolding and manual inspections.

In London’s main financial district, known as the City of London, a virtual-reality model created by the local authority in collaboration with researchers and digital spatial mappers has captured the size and location of every building, window, lamppost and traffic light within the area to within two centimetres of accuracy, allowing planners and the public to properly scrutinize building proposals.

Elsa Arcaute, a complexity science researcher at University College London, cautions against too much faith in digital twins, as a city with all its complexity and interplay between urbanity, nature and human behaviour cannot be completely duplicated.

For most national team coaches, only a keeper who is playing regularly for his club merits consideration.

Unsurprisingly, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is no exception. While he did give Urbig – the backup keeper at Bayern – two starts in his first international break as national team boss, for the upcoming UEFA Nations League matches against Serbia and the Netherlands, Marc-André ter Stegen remains the undisputed No. 1.

But when Klopp gave ter Stegen the nod, Urbig was still spending most of his time on the bench in Munich. But this is set to change after Bayern's recent Bundesliga win over Mainz. The 40-year-old Manuel Neuer asked to be subbed off just before halftime, complaining of severe pain in his right foot.

An examination revealed that Neuer has sustained a partial tendon tear in the foot.

"An injury never comes at the right time, but it's part of the game," Neuer wrote on Instagram.

"I've been through this before, and I'll get through this one too. From now on: full focus on recovery. Until then, I will support the boys on the pitch wherever I can."

A partial tendon tear usually results in a layoff of six to 12 weeks, depending on the severity of the injury. Given that Neuer's foot already has some pre-existing damage from previous injuries, his recovery could take even longer.

Although Urbig is now the de-facto first-choice keeper for Bayern, he will still have to bide his time in the national team as understudy to ter Stegen. However, there is a general consensus that someday, Urbig will also become Germany's No. 1. With Neuer's contract running out in the summer, the chance to truly make the Bayern goal his own appears likely in the not-too-distant future.

The match on Saturday was Neuer's 550th in the Bundesliga and he also became the oldest player in a league match in Bayern's history when he took the pitch aged 40 years and 225 days. In other words, he can't go on forever.

One of his most famous predecessors in the Bayern goal has already called on him to draw a line under his highly successful career.

"I would tell him: 'Call it a day, Manu!' You have given an incredible amount to football, you have won everything, and you don't have to prove anything to anyone anymore," Sepp Maier, a member of West Germany's 1974 World Cup winning team told Sport1.

At some point, the now 82-year-old Maier noted, there comes a moment "when your body no longer behaves the way you want it to. And even a Manuel Neuer cannot stave off that moment."

For now, with ter Stegen playing regularly and performing well for Ajax, Germany coach Klopp is under no pressure to make a change. However, the 34-year-old former Barcelona keeper has, like Neuer, become quite injury-prone in recent years. Whenever he's needed, Urbig will be more than happy to seize his opportunity.

#1016. Xabi Alonso is CONFUSING his Chelsea stars: Blues boss must take his share of the blame as chaos threatens to engulf the club again after deserved defeat by Nottingham Forest, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 17:29 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 18:17 EST, 27 November 2026

It is not yet December and already chaos threatens to engulf Chelsea once more.

A bright start to the season under Xabi Alonso was, it transpires, merely a hazy, late summer mirage. Winter, it seems, will bring only a new version of a classic modern Chelsea discontent.

A coach who has started to do strange things – Alonso selected midfielder Moises Caicedo at centre-half here for the first time in his seven-year club career – a fanbase turning on everyone from the owners to the players and a team slowly getting disorientated on a dismally familiar carousel of selection changes.

It is Chelsea rebooted but just with the same stories written by and for different people. How dismal it must feel for those with this great club in their hearts.

Here on a misty and rainy night at the City Ground, nobody suffered more in Chelsea colours than central defender Wesley Fofana.

Harangued throughout by his own travelling fans for a foolish and unauthorised midweek YouTube interview in which he seemed to make light of missing a penalty in the Carabao Cup defeat at Liverpool, the Frenchman was hauled off soon after conceding a penalty that allowed Morgan Gibbs-White to stretch Nottingham Forest’s lead to two goals early in the second half.

Wesley Fofana was hauled off soon after conceding a penalty that allowed Morgan Gibbs-White to stretch Nottingham Forest’s lead to two goals early in the second half

Fofana was harangued throughout by his own travelling fans for an unauthorised interview in which he seemed to make light of missing a penalty in the Carabao Cup defeat at Liverpool

‘You are not wanted here,’ sang the Chelsea fans and after this they may get their wish. For his own sake, it may be a while before we see the young defender again.

At that stage of the night, Chelsea actually still had hope. Half-time substitute Emmanuel Emegha had just pulled a goal back with his team’s first shot on target of the whole night. He was to get another right at the death, too.

But having started the game with a fabulous fifth minute volley from the Brazilian Igor Jesus – it came off his shin but that doesn’t matter – Forest had the look of a team with their opponents’ measure all evening and that was how it played out. And when Gibbs-White scored his second of the game to make it 3-1 with less than 20 minutes left, Chelsea’s night was pretty much over.

Alonso must certainly take his share of the blame here. Caicedo is his best midfielder but was played out of position with England’s Levi Colwill left on the bench.

Put simply, it backfired. Chelsea’s defending did not improve on recent efforts and in midfield, where they were outplayed by Forest’s Xaver Schlager and James McAtee, they missed the Ecuadorian desperately.

More widely Alonso’s Premier League record – six wins from 12 games – is now worse than that of Liam Rosenior when he was sacked back in April. Their six defeats are one more than Manchester United. And this at a time when Chelsea are playing but once a week. No European competition and out of the Carabao Cup, the Spaniard has plenty of time with his players on the training field. What is he doing with it? Confusing everybody, it would seem, for what Chelsea presented here was a jumble. How they lost by only a goal was a miracle in itself. They deserved nothing.

Forest had come in to the game with issues of their own. Their coach Oliver Glasner had accused his international squad of not making enough effort with their English. Early on their football spoke for them as McAtee spread the play with a wonderful fifth minute pass, Daniel Munoz crossed and Jesus rose to volley his second league goal of the season high past Emiliano Martinez quite wonderfully.

Caicedo is Alonso's best midfielder but the Ecuadorian was played out of position by the Chelsea manager with England’s Levi Colwill left on the bench

Alonso’s Premier League record – six wins from 12 games – is now worse than that of Liam Rosenior when he was sacked back in April

What followed for the rest of the first half did not match that quality. Over time, Alonso’s team did find a way into the game territorially but a free-kick routine that ended with Morgan Rogers ballooning ten yards over the bar perhaps summed their efforts up as indeed did the fact they ended the opening period having managed only three touches inside the Forest box.

Replacing the ineffectual Danny Welbeck with Emegha at the interval brought Chelsea some shape at least. Welbeck had been peripheral. Forest were the team to kick on, though, and when Fofana slipped catastrophically to allow Liam Delap through in the 50th minute, he then brought him down. Gibbs-White slotted in the penalty and Chelsea were in big trouble.

With the away end threatening revolt, Alonso’s team somehow fashioned a lifeline goal from nowhere within four minutes. Pedro Neto’s speculative shot struck Forest defender Jair Cunha on the thigh and when the ball dropped to Emegha, he controlled it instinctively and found the corner.

With Fofana soon withdrawn to doubtless protect his own sanity, Chelsea’s fans now had nothing else to do but support their team. The visitors’ sense of desperation certainly made it a better game but what followed only served to damn Chelsea even more.

Far from the goal imbuing them with the impetus and belief to rescue the game, Alonso’s players somehow allowed Forest to take the initiative once more. There was a fatuous and unsuccessful penalty appeal for handball against Cunha – he had his arms clamped to his side when Rogers’ cross struck him – but precious little else.

And when the generally excellent Austrian Schlager threaded the needle to find Gibbs-White through a crowd with 17 minutes left, the England forward lifted the ball over the advancing Martinez to present a two-goal margin once again.

Chelsea subsequently offered almost nothing only to score – this time with an Emegha header – with two minutes left. Had they added an equaliser it would have been wholly unjust. They didn’t.

#1014. Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

Hitler once called Eastern Europe "Germany's India." A new exhibition examines the links between colonialism and Nazism, and the bitter debate over where comparisons illuminate history and where they fall short.

Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men."

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.

This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

"I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust.

Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people."

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met.

Forced labor was also central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities, for example at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," says Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued."

On October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. But in 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Martinican intellectual Aime Cesaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. More than 70 years later, the exhibition opens amid renewed debates over the definition of settler colonialism and genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over Germany's support for Israel during the war in Gaza and its alleged failure to uphold its obligations under the Genocide Convention to prevent genocide.

These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance.  However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy.

"I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

#1011. How Andoni Iraola made Liverpool's fans - and players - fall in love with him: 'There's a connection building. He gets the club'

Published: 21:00 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 27 November 2026

The first sign that Andoni Iraola was different came this summer in Chicago during Liverpool's pre-season tour.

Sitting in a conference room up in the clouds overlooking the Windy City skyline and out to Lake Michigan, Iraola relaxed into a chair and held court for the best part of an hour. It was his first interview with the assembled Merseyside media corps but felt more laidback and personable than most of those chats tend to.

Most managers have little time for outsiders but Iraola, sipping a black coffee, was happy to stay put and talk about modern football, life in the Basque country and cycling. Only some of that conversation made the cut for the write-up but it all painted a clear picture of the new Liverpool boss.

Four months later, the Anfield faithful are slowly falling in love with Iraola.

It’ll take plenty more time and trophies to reach the adoration they had for Jurgen Klopp but, if Iraola can get halfway to that level, he will have done well.

So ahead of his first Merseyside derby, how has Iraola settled in at Liverpool – and why are the fans taking to him in return?

The Anfield faithful are slowly falling in love with their Spanish manager Andoni Iraola

Iraola takes training in Chicago on Liverpool's pre-season tour. The manager was relaxed during that time despite the pressures of a move to a huge club

It’s the little things that have helped Iraola forge a bond with the Kop.

He has been spotted on the parks of Merseyside taking in Sunday league football. He took his young daughter to a Women’s Super League game and attends her netball matches. And he has taken time to learn about the history of the club and the city, with incognito visits to tourist hotspots.

Iraola and his wife came to Liverpool on a city-break long before he became manager and loved the feel of it; it was a reminder of his hometown Usurbil, near San Sebastian in northern Spain.

He also enjoys cycling, a lifelong hobby, and his helmet helps him go unrecognised on rides around the city.

At the AXA Training Centre, there is a feeling of unity. Virgil van Dijk is a regular at academy matches, Dominik Szoboszlai dropped in on an age-group side last week and first-team players are tutoring youngsters and tracking the teams' scorelines.

None of the above might feel noteworthy in isolation but, to Liverpool fans, these little signs of a joined-up club mean the world. This is a unique fanbase which is often misunderstood: they want people who ‘get’ the club and the city. By immersing himself in them, Iraola is achieving those small wins.

‘There’s definitely a connection building between us and Iraola,’ says Dan Clubbe of fan channel Redmen TV. ‘First and foremost, matters on the pitch are starting to get exciting and the belief is growing as a result.

‘But beyond that, he’s very likeable and although it’s a cliche, he seems to “get it”. Small as they may seem, things like the WSL game, getting out to grassroots footy, integrating youngsters... that all resonates with us as fans.

‘It even goes beyond that. He seems to genuinely love it (here) and wants to understand better the opportunity he’s got, the place that he’s in. It’s still early days but it feels like he realises the significance and responsibility of his position.’

This time last year, the wheels were starting to fall off for Arne Slot. Liverpool felt like a fractured club

Tensions were rumbling around Mohamed Salah, who kicked off publicly and said the club had thrown him ‘under the bus’

This time last year, the wheels were starting to fall off for Arne Slot. Just six months after a Premier League trophy parade through the streets of the city, Liverpool lost 4-1 at home to PSV Eindhoven to record their ninth loss in 12 games, also including a 3-0 defeat by Nottingham Forest at Anfield.

Tensions were rumbling around Mohamed Salah, who in early December kicked off publicly and said the club had thrown him ‘under the bus’. He was dropped from a matchday squad and his relationship with Slot never really recovered. He is now at Turkish side Trabzonspor.

The best way to describe the feeling around the club last season was fractured. Sources point to how Slot kept the same outlook when things were going badly as he did when they were going well.

The place needed a fresh outlook. Iraola was the leading candidate to succeed Slot, though the hierarchy also assessed Pierre Sage, who has since been hired and fired by Crystal Palace, and Sebastian Hoeness of Stuttgart.

The Basque has brought back a feelgood factor to Anfield. Everything feels brighter, smiles are worn more often and even the online naysayers have had to find new things to complain about.

Captain Van Dijk has helped Iraola settle and took the squad to the museum at Anfield a fortnight ago to teach the new signings and academy graduates about the club. Iraola did not join them as he was too busy in the analysis room.

One of Iraola’s assistants, former Bournemouth defender Tommy Elphick, is a big Liverpool fan and that has helped, too. Elphick, alongside fellow assistant Shaun Cooper, has been influential in sorting out a set-piece record that was the worst in the league last season.

Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk has helped Iraola settle into the club

Iraola with assistants Tommy Elphick (left) and Shaun Cooper, who have helped sort out the team's set-piece problems

Elphick and Cooper were with Iraola at Bournemouth and helped him settle into English football after his move from Spanish side Rayo Vallecano.

All of this is helping fans have a better connection with the players, and one small tweak has been to starting holding a team huddle right by the travelling supporters in away games. No team has more away points in the Premier League than Liverpool and Alexander Isak has scored in six straight away trips in all competitions.

It helps that the football is more exciting, too. Isak has scored 10 for the season already and looks a completely different player to the unfit striker that was bereft of confidence last term and managed only four goals.

Florian Wirtz has also been revived and this week publicly thanked Iraola – and his Germany boss Klopp – for helping him rediscover the levels which saw him earn a £116million move to Anfield.

The list goes on: Alexis Mac Allister looked like a man whose best days were behind him but now is back playing like the midfielder who won the World Cup in 2022, while Jeremy Jacquet looks a Rolls-Royce defender in the making. Milos Kerkez is slowly trending upwards.

And then there is Iraola’s faith in youth. Rio Ngumoha, 18, and Trey Nyoni, 19, have been trusted to perform by the new boss. Lewis Koumas and James McConnell have been getting the nod in squads ahead of senior pros Federico Chiesa and Wataru Endo.

Iraola, who is superstitious and tapes his fingers before games for this reason, knows the significance of this week: having thrashed Manchester United and won away in Europe against a decent Club Bruges side, a Merseyside derby win would complete a trio of fantastic results.

Florian Wirtz this week thanked Iraola for helping him rediscover his best level

Iraola has shown faith in youngsters including winger Rio Ngumoha - and he has been repaid handsomely

‘It’s a little bit like here – you know a lot of people on the other side,’ he said on Friday, comparing the clash with Everton to the derby between his boyhood club Athletic Club, of Bilbao, and Real Sociedad, of San Sebastian.

‘I have a lot of friends who are Real Sociedad and they have a lot of friends who are from Athletic.

‘There is always banter throughout the season and everyone wants to finish above them and win the games against them. It’s quite a natural rivalry. The relationship between them is normally quite good but everyone wants to win that game.'

#1007. Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

This article was originally published in German.

#1004. Helsinki puts trust at the heart of its smart-city model

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Benjamin Plackett is a science journalist based in London.

Helsinki Central Library Oodi is just one example of a building in the Finnish capital that uses real-time data to optimize energy efficiency.Credit: Sergei Gapon/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

Urban planners — and curious residents — can go online and click on almost any building in Helsinki to see a host of details including its age, height, heating source and estimated energy use. The information sits in the various maps that make up Helsinki 3D, an open-data digital twin of the city built by the City of Helsinki from aerial photographs, light and detection laser scanning (LiDAR) surveys, housing registers and geographical data. The project’s Energy and Climate Atlas estimates heating demand for nearly every building, models how it would change in response to different climate conditions and calculates the solar-panel potential across every roof and wall in the Finnish capital.

Helsinki’s technical prowess in these kinds of projects is underpinned by a substantial research base; the city is ranked 100th among the world’s top 200 cities in the Nature Index, with particular strength in health sciences (ranked 69th), biological sciences (80th) and Earth and environmental sciences (83rd). It produced 55% of Finland’s total Share in 2025, a ratio that is among the highest for cities in the overall top 200.

The city has treated itself as a laboratory, too. Kalasatama, a brownfield site in the harbour district of Helsinki, has been designated as an urban testbed for researchers, city officials and companies to try out novel urban infrastructure ideas.

Helsinki’s Nordic climate is also an advantage when it comes to handling the large amounts of data involved with smart cities. Cooler air reduces the energy needed to chill large data centres and the excess warmth created by such facilities is redirected to residents using heat pumps. One of the largest data-centre operators that publishes its waste heat recovery data says it recovers up to 90% of its waste heat, which is fed into the district heating network — enough to warm 14,000 two-room apartments.

One of Helsinki’s most distinct smart-city features is the way it uses data.

“We have to be responsible when we use AI. We must do it in a transparent way,” says Pasi Rautio, a service manager for the City of Helsinki’s AI and optimization unit.

The city’s AI register, for example, allows residents to keep tabs on AI projects the city’s government is running. It shows what data are being used and why, and offers the opportunity for public feedback.

#1003. Bayern Munich are at war with themselves over 'unacceptable' treatment of Jamal Musiala, writes CRAIG HOPE - now the £20m-a-year star faces a bitter fight for his future after seizure and injury hell

Published: 02:00 EST, 28 November 2026 | Updated: 02:00 EST, 28 November 2026

It was four years ago this week that I spoke to Lothar Matthaus - and all he wanted to talk about was Jamal Musiala.

The Bayern Munich midfielder was 19 and the poster boy of Germany's impending World Cup campaign in Qatar. Indeed, quite literally, there were posters and shirts bearing Musiala's face and name in Matthaus' Bavarian apartment.

My plan was for the Germany legend to open up on his own World Cup stories, but he enjoyed more slapping me down on Musiala, who had spent much of his childhood in London and played for England Under-21s.

'I like to provoke you again,' he said, having already crowed, playfully, over penalty shootouts. 'You gave the best player from the young English generation to Germany - Jamal Musiala. I have a son who is eight years old. I have to buy the Bayern Munich shirts with No.42 on the back, and I have to buy the Germany shirt with No.14 - my son is crazy about Musiala.

'So, thank you, England, for giving us Musiala. I do not know why you did not fight more to keep this player in the English shirt. We are so happy to have him. When he is on the field, this is like Messi three years ago. He has everything. Fast, good dribbling, the last pass, he can score. He is becoming the complete player. In the future, he will be one of the very best players in the world.'

Today, you wonder which shirt adorns the wall of his son's bedroom. If it is still Musiala, it will be because of loyalty and hope that his father's belief can still be true. That, however, would contrast with the loyalty and belief of Musiala's paymasters at Bayern Munich.

Jamal Musiala has been the subject of a huge row engulfing Bayern Munich this week

The German club's hierarchy have undermined their star and the terms of his contract

For what is playing out in Bavaria right now is an unedifying and divisive debate centred, fundamentally, on the health of a 23-year-old. Musiala has, since April of last year, been under the care of neurological experts after experiencing 'absence-like' symptoms. This only became apparent to the public in August of this year when he collapsed twice in the space of four days during pre-season friendlies.

He revealed a neurological dysfunction but described it as treatable. Last week, away from the cameras, there was another seizure. And then, on Friday of this week, confirmation of a thigh injury that will keep him sidelined for several weeks.

There have been other injuries too, including a broken leg at the 2025 World Club Cup, and a 120mph car accident in April of 2025, for which Musiala lost his license. But also, two months prior, there was a new contract signed until 2030, said to be worth upwards of £20million per year. This, for Bayern, is the complication.

To put it bluntly, Musiala is now paid too much money for what the club gets in return. Since the start of last season, there have been just 14 starts, 16 substitute appearances and seven goals.

'We are in a dilemma,' said Uli Hoeness, Bayern's honorary president, earlier this month. 'He has an illness that cannot easily be cured, but can be managed reasonably well with medication. But whether he will ever again have the level of performance he once had…'

Fellow board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge added his opinion, with all the subtlety of the goals he used to hammer for Bayern and West Germany.

'It's also well known that he has a contract that involves very substantial sums of money,' he said. 'I think it's responsible and completely normal for a club to consider how to handle this. Because then these sums are, of course – sorry, with all due respect – no longer feasible. Unfortunately, what we know suggests that it will be difficult for him to get back to the level he so often showed.'

I was at Bayern's training ground in May. Everywhere, from the club shop to the fencing around the pitches to the messaging in the media suite, are the words - 'Mia san mia'. Translated, the Bayern motto means, 'We are who we are'. At its core is an essence of family, a bond uniting players, staff and supporters. When Vincent Kompany collapsed on the training ground last month, the exhausted head coach was afforded rest and support.

Only, these past couple of weeks have not felt very 'Mia san mia', especially not for Musiala and his family. Nor, it would seem, for his team-mates.

Musiala was viewed as a future star when he first broke onto the scene with the German club

On Wednesday night, after Musiala played the final 14 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 defeat at Lille, captain Joshua Kimmich said: 'The club is always paramount and greater than any individual player - but not greater than the person. That's absolutely unacceptable and not in the spirit of Bayern, which stands for being a family and sticking together. This (Musiala's situation) is something that should have been discussed and resolved together at a table.

'Jamal has our full support 100 per cent, and I'm convinced that he has the club's support as well, even if one or two people have expressed different opinions.'

A truce, of sorts, has since been called.

'FC Bayern and Jamal Musiala's management have agreed to continue their discussions in a spirit of partnership and confidentiality,' said a club statement. 'The player's health is the top priority for both parties. Jamal Musiala will receive full support throughout his recovery.'

At 11am on Tuesday, Musiala's representatives had entered the Sabener Strabe training ground for crisis talks and the above statement was the outcome. It still leaves many more questions than answers, for Musiala and Bayern.

For starters, the treatment of the player risks unsettling and unnerving others in the dressing-room. What if Harry Kane had damaged his ankle ligaments before his new contract was signed, rather than two weeks after? Would Hoeness and Rummenigge have advised against committing to the Ballon d'Or winner? Facetious that may sound, but the thought of contracts being revisited in the event of illness or injury is a dangerous seed to plant.

Since Hoeness' comments surfaced, Bayern have drawn at home to Cologne and lost at Lille. Revelations about goalkeeper Manuel Neuer's private life have hardly helped, either. 'Cheating on pregnant women is a whole different level of evil,' posted his estranged wife. The club is unaccustomed to the headlines of late.

Christian Falk is the head of football at leading tabloid Bild and he has followed Musiala's career, and recent events, as close as anyone. So, what happens now for Musiala?

'That is the biggest question,' he says. 'There are two Bayern Munichs right now. The one Musiala has trust in on the sporting side, including Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl. Then, on the other side, the big bosses, the elder statesmen (Hoeness and Rummenigge). But at Bayern, this is where the decisions are made.

But the diagnosis of a neurological health condition has been a major setback for the star

Insiders say he has not been the same player since his long-term injury owing to a leg break

But his team-mates are rallying around him, with captain Joshua Kimmich branding his bosses' comments as 'unacceptable'

'So while everything now is calm, and Bayern have 'back-pedalled in the boat' and are offering support and help for Musiala, if there is no improvement in the next four to six months, the bosses will talk again. Everyone knows this.'

I was at Bayern's Champions League semi-final second leg against Paris Saint-Germain last season and have revisited my match report, noting the sole comment concerning Musiala, 'one run apart, he struggled'. He was, from memory, peripheral. The game was quicker than him.

Does Falk, then, believe we will ever see Musiala regain or exceed his previous level?

'Kompany has said he was at his very best in training recently,' he says. 'But everyone else is not so sure. It is not just the illness, but also the broken leg. That injury alone would have been enough to impact his level. After that, we have seen that he is not dribbling the same, he does not have the trust in his skills. A lot of the doubt is in his head. If he can remove that, he can be a very, very good player. But the same or better? Maybe not.

'Musiala always had the plan that the next step could be Real Madrid or Manchester City and winning the Ballon d'Or. If he is to be the player he wants to be, the chances are he cannot stay at Bayern, because I don't think he will forget this situation.'

Matthaus has also had his say this week, defending Kimmich.

'I think it was a fantastic interview,' he said. 'Perhaps it didn't sit well with the Bayern bosses, but it should serve as a wake-up call for them to handle situations like this differently in the future. Maybe he will be fined, but you don't resolve things by handing out fines. That would only open up another can of worms. He showed that he is a true captain because he is not only standing up for Musiala, but wants to protect all his players.'

For now, Musiala must protect himself. When he was nine years old at Corpus Christi Catholic Primary School in London, he wrote a poem, 'Moment', which won a competition. One line from that feels very poignant today.

'Suddenly the car stops,' he wrote, referencing his arrival at Chelsea's academy. 'I close my eyes. I take a deep breath. I'm not nervous anymore. I'm happy. I know what I've to do.'

This time, the challenge for Musiala is not to prove how good he can be, but to rediscover how good he was.

#1001. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

#996. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

Enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”

They cannot make anything of set piece and Sunderland have the three points - it wasn’t pretty but they needed the three points and edged the contest.

Questions will be asked of Chelsea now, they were bullied in the first-half and weren’t able to create anything in the second.

Chelsea with the ball inside the Sunderland half. The visitors bring Rogers down and Chelsea have a free-kick. Last-chance sallon for the west Londoners...

Sunderland have a throw inside the Chelsea half - this is about game management for the side in dire need of a win now...

Angulo nrings down his man after a poor pass from Sadiki. The visitors with a free-kick inside their own half.

Emegha drifts past Mukiele before he feels the full force of a Luke O’Nein tackle. It looks as though he gets the ball but the ref awards the free-kick. It’s in the final third, can Chelsea create anything from this?

In short ‘yes’, Estevao delivers a peach of a ball and Welbeck gets on the end of it. BUT his header is over, when it seemed easier to hit the target.

Sunderland in Chelsea half, they’re looking for a free-kick as Angulo goes down. The referee isn’t having any of it...

Sunderland break at pace (only the second time this half) Isador finds Talbi who is free before cutting inside and unleashing a shot from outside the box. It’s just wide, don’t think it was too far away though.

Talbi is off for Angulo, Rigg on for Le Fee for Sunderland, and for Chelsea, Henderson makes way for Emegha.

For all their possession this half Chelsea have not forced Roefs into a meaningful save. Chelsea corner after Geovany Quenda gets in a shot from the left-side of the area that gets a tiny hint of a deflection. Roefs punches away the set-piece and Sunderland breathe a sigh of relief.

Better from Sunderland, there are spaces in behind Chelsea as the visitors go in search of the equaliser and over the past few minutes the hosts have found them.

Lovely ball from Reinildo finds Sadiki in space on the left, they keep the ball brilliantly before Le Fee plays in Isador, it’s a one-on-one and all the Frenchman has to do it dink it over the on-rushing keeper.
