The more things change, the more they stay the same - Watford is an unmanageable club

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some things are certain in life; death, taxes and Watford sacking another head coach.

At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

It was the latest in a series of lifeless performances from a Watford side that have looked ill-equipped for Championship football from the moment the season started.

Now, at a time where Watford need Championship experience more than ever, owner Gino Pozzo has turned to former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu, a man that has had 13 jobs in 15 years, never managed more than 60 games at any team and most importantly, never played or coached in England or in one of Europe’s major leagues.

Given Watford’s reputation with head coaches, many would joke Iordanescu’s appointment sounds like a match made in heaven.

For Hornets fans, though, it’s an act of desperation from a club that has no plan, structure or hope.

In truth, Dionisi is the latest in a series of head coaches who have been let down by owner Pozzo, chairman Scott Duxbury and technical director Gianluca Nani, who seem incapable of building a squad or supporting a head coach.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Things could have been so different for the Italian, because at the start of the season, there was clearly something there. Watford were excellent in their opening day win over Southampton - playing with real flair and intensity in the first half - and followed that up with draws against Wrexham and West Ham. It was clear the players respected the Italian.

However, the warning signs were already there. In the summer, Dionisi and supporters were told that Watford would prioritise experienced players in the transfer market. None arrived.

Nestory Irankunda, Imran Louza and Giorgi Chakvetadze - three key players - were sold and not replaced, with Watford starting the season with just two centre-backs on the club’s books and two fit central midfielders.

The Italian sounded increasingly exasperated as his calls for reinforcements fell on deaf ears until the final few days of the window, where Watford eventually panicked and brought in Stephy Mavididi, Soumaila Coulibaly and Branimir Mlacic on loan. Myron Boadu and Michail Antonio arrived on free transfers.

Most of those players arrived unfit and come September, Dionisi was struggling to fill the bench as injuries took hold. The Italian never really recovered from embarrassing defeats to Burnley and Cardiff City, deploying a back five in recent weeks as he attempted to make the Golden Boys harder to beat.

Quite frankly, Watford are unmanageable. Not even Pep Guardiola would be successful at Vicarage Road, because no head coach is given the opportunity to implement a style of play when they have to contend with poor recruitment, a leadership vacuum and a dressing room with seemingly poor attitudes.

Rob Edwards was promised he'd be backed in the transfer market come hell or high water by chairman Duxbury in the summer of 2022. Most of the signings he received didn't fit his system and he was sacked within two months of the season starting.

After Edwards, Slaven Bilic thought he'd be able to sign players he wanted in the January transfer window. He received Joao Ferreira and Henrique Araujo - both of whom never looked suited to Championship football – as well as Ryan Porteous, Wesley Hoedt and Britt Assombalonga. Bilic was gone by March.

Then came Chris Wilder, who repeatedly called out the poor attitude within the dressing room and wasn't given a contract extension when his deal expired in the summer of 2023. After the wheels came off under Valerian Ismael, Tom Cleverley was promoted to head coach in 2024 and despite a thin squad, united the players and fans, having been a popular player at Vicarage Road during his playing days.

Once again, though, January arrived and Cleverley didn't get the options he so dearly needed, meaning Watford's form dropped off and he was sacked, somewhat harshly, at the end of the season.

Just last season, the popular Javi Gracia returned for a second spell in charge and had Watford in the play-off spots by January. He was promised additions, but none were forthcoming and ultimately the Spaniard decided the job wasn't worth his time. Gracia resigned, returning to Spain to spend time with his family.

In short, it's time the Watford ownership took a long, hard look at themselves, rather than the head coach. Has Iordanescu been appointed because no one sensible will take it? Any head coach worth his salt in England - and possibly now Italy, too - knows what they’re walking into.

In a recent interview with Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement, Pozzo tried shifting accountability for the club’s downfall, which can be traced back to the FA Cup Final in 2019. Since then, numerous decisions have, in the eyes of supporters, led to the erosion of the club's identity - fans have had enough.

Empty statements, the constant churn of players and head coaches, and what appears to be a lack of any real structure or plan - supporters are fed up.

The fact Watford closed their Under-21 setup, downgraded their academy and sold off the women's team this summer was a huge source of disappointment for fans, too, given the club’s rich history of bringing players through their youth system.

Unless there is a sudden change of approach overnight, Watford are only heading one way and that's down to League 1.

Bradley is a sports journalist and Watford fan, who previously spent seven years working for talkSPORT. In his spare time, he is the commentator for Non League side Harefield United. Previously, he worked for Newsquest, covering both Watford and Leyton Orient for the Watford Observer and East London Guardian Series newspapers. He has also had pieces published in the Daily Mail and Watford's matchday programme.

#880. Leeds climb into top six with dominant Coventry win

Leeds United vs Coventry City. Premier League.

Report and free match highlights as Leeds beat Coventry 3-0 at Elland Road; Dominic Calvert-Lewin celebrates new contract with a goal as Sean Longstaff also scores twice; win sees Daniel Farke's side climb into the Premier League top six

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Leeds' European push continued in a dominant 3-0 victory over Coventry.

In a week where several new contract extensions were celebrated, there was even more joy for the Elland Road faithful as Daniel Farke's men put on a complete display to break into the top six of the table.

Coventry had been warned about Leeds' set-piece threat, with James Justin and Ethan Ampadu going close from corners. They failed to learn their lesson though as Calvert-Lewin, 48 hours after signing a contract extension, was left unmarked to head home from a free-kick.

The visitors remained at sixes and sevens as the advantage was doubled five minutes later courtesy of a Tatsuhiro Sakamoto deflection from Sean Longstaff's effort.

From then on, Coventry were more or less out of the contest, confirmed by Longstaff's second which was set-up by a glorious back heel from Gabriel Gudmundsson.

Victory means that Leeds have lost just seven Premier League games since switching to a back three 364 days ago against Manchester City. As a result, they sit sixth in the table, just two points off Man City in third.

18: CHANCE! Calvert-Lewin wastes huge opportunity by opting to pass instead of shoot.

28: OVER! Ampadu balloons close range effort over the bar.

40: GOAL! New contract, same result! Calvert-Lewin finally puts Leeds ahead.

45: GOAL! Deflected Longstaff strike doubles the hosts advantage.

53: SAVE! Calvert-Lewin opens up for the far corner but Rushworth reads it to keep him out.

58: WIDE! Okafor looks to find the far corner but his shot doesn't have enough curl.

65: GOAL! Incredible Gudmundsson assist allows Longstaff to double tally.

69: SAVE! Bogle denied a Leeds fourth by Rushworth.

Leeds boss Daniel Farke speaking post-match:

"These are the type of games that you have to win because after such an amazing win [against Chelsea], everyone is buzzing and it is such a passionate club that you can also get carried away. Thinking okay, home game against a newly promoted side, here we go.

"No, these types of games are the most difficult ones and we showed a good mentality. We were fully focussed and switched on, showed great maturity. We also found during the game a few other gears after perhaps not the best start. Overall, a pretty dominant performance.

"After a great win, to show this consistency again, that's what pleased me most today."

Coventry boss Frank Lampard speaking post-match:

"It was a pivotal moment in the game [conceding before half-time]. Until that point, we were OK in terms of shape. Dealing with Leeds' strengths which we set out to try and stop. They're a big crossing team and have a lot of players running through our backline with real energy.

"I think we slowed the game down which is what we wanted to do and had a couple moments on the counter-attack. But the goals are errors from us. Things that can't happen. We're in the Premier League now and it's critical. It changed the feel of the game. From then on, it was very difficult for us.

"I was happy [with how the team played in a back three]. Leeds are established in the Premier League. You know you're coming up against strengths so we were trying to counteract them. I thought we counteracted it well. The message at half-time was the issue wasn't tactically. It was switching off in moments. Of course, the second half becomes harder.

"Big learning for the lads there. We haven't had that this season really."

Saturday's win comes almost a year to the day since Daniel Farke opted to switch to a back three midway through an away defeat at Manchester City and from then on, everything has changed.

Since putting that new system in place, Farke's men have lost just seven Premier League matches. They've played 37. Only Arsenal, Man City and Bournemouth have lost fewer if you exclude teams that didn't feature in the top flight in both the 2025/26 and 2026/27 seasons (Hull and Ipswich).

They have also picked up three league wins on the bounce, something they haven't managed in the top flight since 2021. For Farke, it's a feat he had never previously achieved himself.

This is a manager who looked destined to lose his job before a ball had even been kicked last season. Yet, he now stands on the verge of a new contract. Better yet, he is letting fans dream of European football for the first time in over two decades.

What a way to celebrate the anniversary of Farke's most pivotal call of his career.

Getting promoted is always going to bring challenges for any side. And picking up results away from home as a newly promoted outfit is a difficult ask.

If you're Frank Lampard though, you need to find a way to do it sooner rather than later.

Coventry have picked up just one away win from six, that being against Nottingham Forest. The rest have all been defeats.

Yes, there have been trips to Arsenal and Man City in there, which 99.9 per cent of people would've had them down to lose comfortably. The issue is, they were swept aside far easier at Elland Road than they were at the Emirates or the Etihad especially.

Results like this one and the one against Everton could be costly as the season progresses. They could be games in which Lampard looks back and thinks 'if only we nicked something here.'

Their home form is bailing them out at the moment, but if that dries up, Coventry need to find a way to turn some of these away defeats into draws at a minimum.

#878. Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

Germany's fall from grace in recent years has seen the team drift away from the fans. But Monday's drubbing of the Netherlands and the impact of Jürgen Klopp, Florian Wirtz and emerging youngsters offers hope.

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves."

The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp said after the Netherlands match.

"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired."

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.

Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong."

Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer."

While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it."

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.

In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

#877. What is the Riemann hypothesis? A guide to the famed conjecture that rules prime numbers

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

German mathematician Bernhard Riemann formulated his famous conjecture in 1859.Credit: Smithsonian Libraries and Archives (CC0)

On 20 November, mathematicians made two competing announcements about solving the Riemann hypothesis — perhaps the most important open problem in mathematics.

The question had remained unanswered since it was formulated in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann (1826–66). His statement is central to the theory of prime numbers, the whole numbers that cannot be evenly divided by any other number except themselves or 1.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The hypothesis concerns the distribution of primes, and it is important because these numbers are central to all of maths. “There is nothing more basic and more fundamental in mathematics that the prime numbers,” says Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a mathematician at the University of Connecticut in Storrs.

Riemann arrived at his idea by studying prime numbers as waves — in a way that presages the way music recordings are compressed into mp3 files — and his hypothesis is usually described in abstruse-sounding language. But at its heart, the idea boils down to a statistical test that is familiar to any scientist who’s ever analysed data.

Nature breaks down the Riemann hypothesis.

Mathematicians want to know how predictable the prime numbers are. The German scientist Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855), who many consider to be the greatest mathematician in history, had noticed in the late eighteenth century (when he was a teenager) that if you pick any whole number, the odds that it’s a prime depend on the number’s size. Primes slowly become sparser as numbers become bigger. Gauss observed that their frequency seems to depend on (or, is inversely proportional to) the number of digits. Roughly speaking, among numbers with k digits, one in every k of them is a prime.

In Riemann’s time, a half-century after Gauss’s guess, there was still no rigorous proof of this. In a landmark paper in 1859, Riemann stated his belief that the late Gauss, who had been one of his mentors at the University of Göttingen, had been right.

But Riemann — who was a “daring” thinker, says maths historian Rossana Tazzioli at the University of Lille in France — went much further. He proposed that Gauss’s “one in every k” guess was a good statistical prediction, meaning that the frequency of the primes should not fluctuate away from it too much. In other words, Riemann made a guess about the margin of error of Gauss’s prediction.

If true, this ‘Riemann hypothesis’ would make primes’ behaviour similar to that of a random process, such as a series of coin tosses. More precisely, he suggested that when you count the primes among the first n whole numbers, fluctuations would take a form that many scientists are familiar with: “The idea of the Riemann hypothesis is that the error term looks a lot like √n, which is what any random model will give you,” says Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

Such square-root terms pop up everywhere in data analysis, because they control the shrinking of a margin of error as the number n of data points grows.

In his paper, Riemann did much more than guess. He introduced tools that would constitute the basis for much of the work on number theory — the branch of mathematics that concerns integers, primes and divisibility — in the following centuries.

First, by developing new techniques in analysis — another word for advanced calculus — as he went along, Riemann constructed the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter ‘zeta’).

Riemann then showed that the function embodied an enormous amount of information about prime numbers. First, he proved that the solutions to the equation ζ (z) = 0 — where z is a point on a plane — encode the statistical distribution of prime numbers along the number line. To do so, Riemann employed a type of Fourier analysis, the type of maths that nowadays enables the compression of music into compact mp3 files by breaking sound waves down into sinusoidal components.

#874. Alonso crisis deepens as chaotic Chelsea lose and fans taunt own player

It always feels like Chelsea are not far away from a crisis and Xabi Alonso has now lost more Premier League games this season than Manchester United.

Alonso will inevitably come under further scrutiny after another alarming result and performance, with unpopular centre-back Wesley Fofana also targeted by Chelsea’s supporters.

Chants of “f--- off Fofana, you’re not wanted here” were clearly heard from the away end after another excruciating experience for the defender.

After an ill-advised interview earlier this week, Fofana followed that up with a string of mistakes which led to Nottingham Forest’s second goal.

Forest have secured 11 of their 12 points against clubs in the perceived “Big Six” and Aston Villa, who are competing in the Champions League, and did not deserve the scoreline to be as close.

Alonso is the latest Chelsea manager to become embroiled in chaos before Christmas and four defeats from five league matches will not make happy reading for the hierarchy.

His defence appear to be nervous wrecks and in his desperation to toughen them up he opted to play Moisés Caicedo in what was a peculiar line-up.

Chelsea have conceded 23 goals in the league and until they improve that record, Alonso will find it impossible to retain the club’s backing.

“Everyone in the club needs to stick together and we have to deal with it,” he said. “We are going through a difficult moment with solidity and confidence, we need to find solutions.

“Everyone in the team is needed and I am thinking about the next games and we will see [if Fofana is picked for the next game]. We need to support everyone and if we don’t, things will get more complicated.”

Forest responded after their insipid performance at Bournemouth last weekend to secure another notable home result for Oliver Glasner.

He must be hoping that Forest’s owner, Evangelos Marinakis, turns up for every game.

Marinakis was in attendance for only the second time this season and, on his last visit, witnessed a stirring victory over Manchester City.

Morgan Gibbs-White scored twice to win the private battle of the England No 10s, with Chelsea’s Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers both ineffective.

Glasner said: “We feel we are heading in the right direction but there is still a lot to do. Twelve points from 12 games is still not satisfying for us, but wins like this help us show the players that it is working.

“If you have back-to-back wins against City and Chelsea you must be doing many things really well.”

Xaver Schlager provides a beautiful assist for Morgan Gibbs-White to restore Nottingham Forest's two-goal lead 🎯 https://t.co/zpkElGvNJy

While Glasner is seeing clear signs of progress, the problems are piling up for Alonso.

He has managed only one fewer league game than his predecessor Liam Rosenior and his record so far is equally underwhelming.

This was always likely to be a long-term project and Chelsea remain convinced Alonso will lead them into a bright new era.

For now, it appears that he will have to endure some very tough moments.

The January transfer window has annually proved a solution for struggling Chelsea managers in the past, but where does Alonso even start with this team?

He seems to have many problems to solve and there is no greater concern than the state of his defence.

Levi Colwill was dropped and Caicedo, who has made his name in the Premier League as a midfielder, was drafted in as an emergency centre-back.

Alongside Caicedo was Fofana, retaining his place despite a sloppy performance against Leeds and an unauthorised interview in which he appeared to laugh off his penalty miss at Liverpool in the Carabao Cup.

Fofana was booed throughout by the travelling fans and that reception perfectly captured the sense of disconnect at the club right now.

Only five minutes had elapsed when Chelsea conceded their latest goal, though it was a sublime finish from Igor Jesus, Forest’s £16.5m signing from Botafogo.

After some neat play between Jair Cunha and James McAtee in front of the Chelsea penalty area, Daniel Muñoz floated an inviting cross towards Jesus who volleyed the ball into the corner.

"It's a WORLDIE!" Igor Jesus with a wonderful strike to give Nottingham Forest the lead against Chelsea! 🚀 https://t.co/k8kYQACVdz

Glasner has overseen an equally frustrating start, even though much of the data points to a team overperforming without the results to match.

Outstanding against Manchester City, but awful against Bournemouth, these type of tactical games seem to suit his players better. Whereas there were questions over Alonso’s set-up, Glasner was shrewd.

Forest increased their lead in the 51st minute after a nightmarish sequence of events for Fofana.

Delap capitalised on a mistake from the Frenchman to advance towards the penalty area and as he shaped to shoot he was brought down by the defender

Fofana was booked and Gibbs-White stepped up to put away his second goal of the season.

Morgan Gibbs-White doubles Nottingham Forest's lead! 🔴 https://t.co/DwZQk7OdZ7

Game over? Not so. Emmanuel Emegha, a substitute, pounced after a fortuitous deflection off Cunha to stroke the ball into the corner.

As the goal was reviewed by VAR for offside, Chelsea’s fans again vented their anger with Fofana.

Those expletive-laden chants were clear and loud during the pause in play, and he was taken off in the 56th minute.

Chelsea frustration increased 17 minutes from the end when Gibbs-White poked the ball past Emiliano Martínez after a clever pass from Xaver Schlager.

The London side did respond with another goal from Emegha, this time a header from Pedro Neto’s cross, but they have now lost more games than any Premier League team (14) since March 1.

"He's at it again!" Emmanuel Emegha scores his second of night to set up a nervy finish for Nottingham Forest 👀 https://t.co/XSExh2YLds

Picking Fofana backfired when the defender failed to win over the away fans with a sloppy performance.

Checking the opinions of supporters online, it appears the decision has done little to convince them that Alonso is their man.

Speaking to Sky Sports about the player, he said: “We need to support everyone. Everyone that is in the team we need to support. We know we have to go through difficult moments and we don’t take apart anyone and we want to help and stick together.”

Thank you for reading tonight, and that is it for our live coverage of the game.

Chelsea are never far away from a crisis and this feels like a big night for Xabi Alonso.

Three defeats in the last four Premier League games, including a thrashing by Leeds in their last match, has cranked up the pressure.

This was always likely to be a long-term project, however, and Chelsea remain convinced Alonso will lead them into a bright new era.

Until then, there are going to be some tricky times ahead. Chelsea are as wildly unpredictable as the team they face this evening at the City Ground.

They would leapfrog Coventry regardless of the margin of victory, as they already have a better goal difference.

A draw would see them remain 17th, while a really heavy defeat might see them fall to 18th.

Glasner conceded, in his own press conference, that he had hoped for better results so far this season.

He said: “We wanted and expected more to be honest, but it is still early. We look at what we need to improve and work on it. I’m no magician, I have no dust I can spread at the training ground.

“From my experience, everything is hard work and we need to improve our individual mistakes and defence. We need to improve our efficiency in attack and set pieces. We still haven’t scored from a set piece.”

He added that the club wanted a good atmosphere for the evening kick-off, saying that, “is what we want and need. Friday night under the flood lights - it’s crucial. Our fans want a great weekend.”

Earlier in the week, Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana said he could now “laugh” about a recent penalty miss against Liverpool in the Carabao Cup.

While the statement went down badly amongst some supporters, Fofana has apologised, and Alonso told a pre-match press conference he was ready to move on.

He told journalists: “Absolutely, we have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate.

“He apologised, he knows it was not right the moment, it was not right the content, we are here to take things seriously and he said that it’s not going to be repeated and we know that it’s something that we don’t want, these kind of things, and they are not going to be repeated for sure.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea.

The City Ground hosts the Premier League clash tonight, with two sides who are both falling short of expectations.

Forest head coach Oliver Glasner brought with him a sense of optimism after he left Crystal Palace, but the club are just outside the bottom three, sitting in 17th position with only nine points. As things stand, they are only clear of 18th-placed Sunderland because of superior goal difference.

Beneath them, Glasner’s former club Palace are bottom, two points away from them, and then Manchester United come in 19th, a single point behind. With Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino now installed at Selhurst Park and Old Trafford, respectively, the pressure could soon be felt yet more keenly.

There have been flashes of encouragement, with a 3-1 win over Manchester City in early November, spearheaded by a brace from Liam Delap, who left Chelsea in the summer. However, last Saturday they lost 2-0 at Bournemouth to dent any nascent momentum, and the match was the sixth in 11 league games where the club have failed to score. Forest have scored nine times this season, with only Sunderland having a worse record in attack.

Chelsea’s Xabi Alonso has also endured a tough time of late. They were trounced 4-1 against Leeds United at home on Saturday, despite taking the lead in the first half.

That worrying collapse was the fourth loss in five league matches, and it followed a 1-0 defeat against Sunderland at the Stadium of Light before the recent international break.

There is speculation that Chelsea will move for a central defender in January, with 20 goals conceded in the Premier League so far.

Chelsea are currently in eighth place in the league with 16 points, five points behind Liverpool in fourth. Tonight, they could leapfrog Bournemouth, who are in fifth, two points ahead of them. Another loss, though, could see them in the bottom half once the weekend’s fixtures are completed.

#871. Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair

Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.

This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.

The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month.

Since Huang's resignation, some investors — including Elon Musk and Donald Trump — have voiced concern that his departure could leave Nvidia and America's AI sector in peril and are now calling for his return. Huang on Tuesday, expressed regret for "serious mistakes" in his personal life before declaring he would be "honored" to return if the company's board of directors thought that was "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."

Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).

The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.

Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.

The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.

The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.

"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea."

Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.

Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.

That company, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

It might get worse before it gets better for Manchester City fans

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Never be the man after ‘the man’, the saying goes. Football history is stippled with cautionary tales of managers who followed an all-time great, only to discover that they were doomed from the very beginning.

Manchester City have stumbled through a bruising autumn under Enzo Maresca, uncharacteristically so. It is impossible not to wonder if the Etihad Stadium is experiencing its very own version of Manchester United's 2013/14.

For a decade, Pep Guardiola bent English football to his will, turning Man City into a relentless, trophy-winning machine. Succeeding a figure who loomed so large over the east side of Manchester was never going to be straightforward. Few, though, expected the drop-off to feel quite so jarring, or quite so familiar.

David Moyes arrived at Old Trafford in 2013 tasked with prolonging Sir Alex Ferguson’s dynasty, meanwhile Maresca was handed a three-year contract this summer to keep Guardiola’s juggernaut in motion. Four months into the job, the steering wheel is juddering uncomfortably.

Man City’s recent results make for grim reading compared to the standards set over the last 10 years. A 3-1 defeat away at Nottingham Forest earlier this month was double-take worthy, before Saturday’s 1-1 home draw with Fulham - rescued only by an Elliot Anderson volley - saw them lose yet more ground in the Premier League title race.

On Tuesday night in the Champions League, Man City needed an 86th-minute Rayan Cherki strike just to salvage a 2-2 draw at home to Napoli, currently eighth in Serie A and 14 points off the pace.

Ahead of Sunday’s trip to league leaders Arsenal, Maresca's men look a shadow of the team that so recently struck fear into the Gunners' title hopes.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Predictably, the question of Maresca’s future has already begun to take on more of a 'when rather than if' feel. Reports emerged this week suggesting the Italian is fighting to save his job barely a third of the way into his debut Etihad campaign. Sack talk at Manchester City circulating at all, never mind in November, speaks volumes about how rapidly things have changed.

There are parallels between Man City’s recent slump and Moyes’ 10-month spell across town, too. Like Moyes, Maresca inherited a squad undergoing significant churn after an era of dominance.

To bridge that gap, City made a throng of big summer purchases, bringing in additions such as Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernandez, Iliman Ndiaye and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

Much like Moyes’ integration of Marouane Fellaini and Juan Mata into a fading champion side, Maresca’s new-look Man City feels disjointed - caught between Guardiola’s positional automatisms and a new manager’s attempt to stamp his own authority on the dressing room.

That disconnect quickly becomes apparent when the team aren't getting results, breeding doubt among players accustomed to certainty and success. All of which begs the question: was Maresca always doomed to fail?

Following Guardiola was always going to be an exercise in managing impossible expectations while rebuilding in real time. Perhaps the Etihad hierarchy believed their structure would insulate Guardiola’s successor from the same sort of post-Ferguson collapse that swallowed Moyes' efforts - which in hindsight weren't all that bad. Perhaps there is a lesson there for Man City chiefs to heed.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#869. Burnley claim second win of season at free-falling Millwall

Millwall vs Burnley. EFL Championship.

Report and free match highlights from the Sky Bet Championship match between Millwall and Burnley at the Den; Jaydon Banel's deflected shot gave Burnley just their second victory of the season

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jaydon Banel's deflected shot gave Burnley just their second victory of the season in the Sky Bet Championship as they won 1-0 at Millwall, whose own campaign is lurching from bad to worse.

A first win in nine games for the Clarets was also their first under head coach Fabio Celestini and they are now just two points off Lincoln in 21st place.

For the Lions, however, this was a fifth defeat in a row and they were booed off by their supporters at the final whistle as they continue to slide towards danger.

In a match between two out-of-form sides, it was Millwall who started the more confidently, with Lyndon Dykes sending a half-volley wide after Burnley had failed to clear their lines.

Against the run of play, it was the Clarets who had the game's first big chance after 18 minutes when Josh Laurent played in Andreas Hountondji whose shot across goal was tipped behind by Millwall goalkeeper Lukas Jensen.

That opportunity seemed to settle the visitors down, with Largie Ramazani then trying his luck from distance and Jensen being needed to beat his effort away.

But the next opening came for the Lions as Daniel Kelly found Dykes in space just inside the area, and the Scotland striker's shot was pushed out by Burnley goalkeeper Max Weiss.

Birmingham 2-4 Bolton: Goalkeeper James Beadle sent off as Blues miss opportunity in Championship promotion hopes

Derby 0-0 Watford: Edward Iordanescu's held to a goalless draw in first Hornets game

West Brom 1-0 Bristol City: Jimmy-Jay Morgan scores a late winner after Robins substitute Lisav Eissat sent off

Wrexham 1-0 Portsmouth: Callum Doyle extends Phil Parkinson's side unbeaten run in the Championship

West Ham 1-0 Stoke: Konstantinos Mavropanos scores winner as Scott Parker gets first win as Hammers boss despite Jarrod Bowen injury

QPR 1-1 Sheffield United: Kalvin Phillips sent off as QPR rescue draw against Blades

Luke Cundle then bent an effort over the bar for the hosts who were beginning to exert the sort of pressure they had earlier in the first half.

But Burnley threatened an opener again three minutes before half-time when Ramazani drove into the penalty area before his powerful shot from a narrow angle was turned behind by Jensen.

It was Millwall's turn to come close again 11 minutes into the second half when Caleb Taylor's header down found Kyrell Lisbie, whose shot was fumbled by Weiss, with the German able to beat Camiel Neghli to the rebound.

The Clarets then snatched the lead in the 59th minute when half-time substitute Banel was not closed down sufficiently as he advanced into the area and his shot was deflected into the far corner.

Josh Coburn was immediately thrown on by Millwall boss Alex Neil and had the ball in the net a few minutes later from Lisbie's pass but was correctly flagged offside.

The Lions' need for an equaliser was becoming desperate, but Coburn was unable to keep a header from Mark Sykes' cross down.

Burnley almost made the game safe when Banel was again able to wander into the Millwall area unchallenged and his shot was pushed out by Jensen before Ramazani miscued the rebound wide.

Laurent then shot wide after getting in behind Zak Sturge, but the Clarets comfortably held out for what they hope will be a campaign-altering victory.

"We performed well in the first half and performed alright, I thought, for large parts of the second half, probably until we started to make changes to go for the game.

"That was probably my biggest frustration because instead of us getting better and getting a head of steam and trying to pressurise them, I thought we got weaker at that point and they looked more likely to score than we did.

"When you're making more aggressive changes and you're bringing more attacking players onto the pitch, you'd like to think it would have the opposite effect.

"What isn't helpful is the fact we were playing pass-the-parcel along our backline when we've got two centre-forwards up the pitch, so that wasn't very good.

"I thought the more changes we made, the poorer we got and I was really disappointed with the last 15 minutes of the match when we went two up front."

"It's a good feeling. When you have a new job, you are waiting for your first game, winning, for everything.

"It's special at every club, but I think in this moment it's a special sensation and I'm very happy for the team.

"We knew what we were expecting here; long ball, second ball, free-kicks, corners, a difficult challenge every time.

"I don't think we had a great game with the ball, but the most important thing was the fighting spirit."On Jamie Vardy's omission: "I talked with Jamie yesterday, telling him he would not be in the squad for this game.

"Every six months, Jamie has some injections in his back - because he has spasms - and we did that during the international break, 10 days ago.

"He lost two or three training [sessions] because of this injection and he felt pain in the last two or three days and we decided together to give him rest."
